content: The number of events recorded in the studies is insufficient to confidently estimate the effect size. A systematic review included studies such as Sagara 2018 (Bougoula, Mali), Sagara 2018 (Kolle, Mali), Tshefu 2010, Sagara 2018 (Sotuba, Mali), Sagara 2018 (Bobo-Dioulasso, Burkina Faso), Kayentao 2012, and Roth 2018a. The baseline or comparator used was the control arm of reference for the intervention. There was no serious inconsistency observed. However, there was serious indirectness as the trials included both adults and children, with sites in Africa and Asia. Notably, only 115 children and no adults were randomized to ASPY in Asia. Imprecision was also serious. Another systematic review included studies such as Sagara 2018 (Kolle, Mali), Roth 2018a, Kayentao 2012, Tshefu 2010, Sagara 2018 (Sotuba, Mali), Sagara 2018 (Bouguola, Mali), and Sagara 2018 (Bobo-Dioulasso, Burkina Faso). The baseline or comparator was the control arm of reference for the intervention. No serious inconsistency was noted, but there was serious indirectness. The trials included both adults and children, with sites in Africa and Asia. However, only 115 children and no adults were randomized to ASPY in Asia. Imprecision was serious, as the confidence intervals (CIs) included both no effect and clinically significant effects. Based on data from 3,130 participants in three studies, the difference was 5 per 1,000, with one fewer per 1,000 (95% CI: 4 fewer to 6 more). The evidence was rated as low due to serious indirectness and serious imprecision. It is unclear if there is a difference in bilirubin levels between ASPY and AL. WHO guidelines for malaria (16 October 2023) state that the evidence is insufficient to determine this. A systematic review included studies such as Sagara 2018 (Mafrinyah, Guinea), Sagara 2018 (Bouguola, Mali), Sagara 2018 (Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso), Sagara 2018 (Kolle, Mali), Sagara 2018 (Djoliba, Mali), and Sagara 2018 (Sotuba, Mali). The baseline or comparator was the control arm of reference for the intervention. No serious inconsistency was observed, but there was serious indirectness. The data were drawn from one study conducted in six sites across three countries in West Africa. Imprecision was serious. Based on data from 1,245 participants in one study, the difference was 4 per 1,000, with four fewer per 1,000 (95% CI: 7 fewer to 14 more). The evidence was rated as low due to serious indirectness and serious imprecision. Compared to AS-AQ, ASPY may have fewer PCR-adjusted failures at day 28. Based on data from 1,091 participants in one study, the difference was 5 per 1,000, with no fewer per 1,000 (95% CI: 5 fewer to 23 more). The evidence was rated as low due to serious indirectness and serious imprecision. There may be little or no difference in PCR-adjusted failures at day 42 between ASPY and AS-AQ. Based on data from 1,257 participants in one study, the difference was 37 per 1,000, with 38 fewer per 1,000 (95% CI: 52 fewer to 14 fewer). The evidence was rated as moderate due to serious indirectness. Compared to AS-AQ, ASPY probably has fewer unadjusted failures at day 28. Based on data from 1,059 participants in one study, the difference was 70 per 1,000, with 13 fewer per 1,000 (95% CI: 38 fewer to 26 more). The evidence was rated as low due to serious indirectness and serious imprecision. There is probably little or no difference in unadjusted failures at day 42 between ASPY and MQ+AS. A systematic review included studies such as Rueangweerayut 2012. The baseline or comparator was the control arm of reference for the intervention. No serious inconsistency was observed, but there was serious indirectness. The data were drawn from one study conducted in six sites across three countries in West Africa. Imprecision was serious. Based on data from 1,271 participants in one study, the difference was 18 per 1,000, with 13 more per 1,000 (95% CI: 0 fewer to 111 more). The evidence was rated as low due to serious indirectness and serious imprecision. Compared to MQ+AS, ASPY may lead to higher events of abnormal ALT increase. Aggregate analysis indicates this estimate may be accurate. Based on data from 1,271 participants in one study, the difference was 0 per 1,000, with 0 fewer per 1,000 (95% CI: 0 fewer to 0 fewer). The evidence was rated as very low due to very serious imprecision and serious indirectness. It is unclear if there is a difference in AST levels between ASPY and MQ+AS. Based on data from 1,271 participants in one study, the difference was 7 per 1,000, with 5 more per 1,000 (95% CI: 1 fewer to 55 more). The evidence was rated as very low due to serious indirectness and very serious imprecision. WHO guidelines for malaria (16 October 2023) state that there is probably little or no difference in the rate of serious adverse events with ASPY compared to other antimalarials. Based on data from 3,941 participants in seven studies, the difference was 7 per 1,000, with one more per 1,000 (95% CI: 2 fewer to 9 more). The evidence was rated as moderate due to serious imprecision. Abnormal ALT increase is more frequent with ASPY compared to other antimalarials. Based on data from 6,669 participants in eight studies, the difference was 7 per 1,000, with 5 more per 1,000 (95% CI: 2 more to 13 more). The evidence was rated as high.
